Sampled-negative accuracy does not establish full-catalog top-list quality. [Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) show sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation. [RecSys 2025 research](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086) distinguishes sampling fidelity, resolution, robustness and predictive power; uniform and popularity-based candidate distributions can produce different conclusions. A [2024 sequential-recommendation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) also finds aggregate results conceal head/mid/tail disparities. [Hard-BPR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19276) highlights false-negative risk: difficult unobserved items can be potential positives, so semantic-neighbor failures cannot automatically be interpreted as preference errors.

Practical diagnostic synthesis: freeze training-only prefix–next-item examples and compare equal-sized, unique distractor sets drawn uniformly, proportional to training interaction frequency, and from title/description TF-IDF neighbors. Record candidate IDs, sampler probabilities or similarity scores, seed, exclusions, metadata coverage and fallback counts; exclude padding, target and prefix items. Flag distractors appearing later in the available training history as known-positive conflicts; other unobserved items remain ambiguous. Report target HR@10, reciprocal rank and score margins by prefix length and training-frequency band, with user/example counts and uncertainty. For a fixed subset, score the eligible catalog in chunks using the same single trained NextItNet, counting scores above the target to obtain exact target ranks with explicit tie handling; report rank quantiles, full-catalog HR@10 and sampled/full hit disagreement. Treat these as training diagnostics with possible memorization, not independent generalization estimates. Preserve the pinned validation evaluator and four-category macro HR@10 selection unchanged.
